Resting metabolic rate measurements for Nyctophilus bifax were obtained from individuals maintained under standard thermoneutral conditions. At a body temperature of 34.8 °C [T = 34.8 °C], the maximum basal metabolic rate was recorded at 12.67 milliliters of oxygen per hour [JOi = 12.67 milliliters of oxygen per hour], a value that aligns closely with predictions for a vespertilionid bat of its size. This elevated oxygen consumption likely reflects the energetic demands of maintaining homeothermy during active periods. Neonatal individuals, based on comparative data from the congener Plecotus auritus, emerge with a wet weight at birth of 2.6 grams [Wwb = 2.6 grams], a modest mass that underscores the altricial state of the newborn pups. The combination of a relatively high mass-specific metabolic rate and a small birth mass suggests that females face considerable energetic costs during the early stages of lactation, a pattern commonly observed among insectivorous bats.

Female Nyctophilus bifax attain an ultimate wet weight of approximately 12 grams [Wwi = approximately 12 grams] upon reaching somatic maturity, a body size that places them among the smaller members of the Vespertilionidae. This adult mass is achieved following a period of sustained juvenile growth, during which the suckling juveniles rely entirely on maternal milk. The transition to nutritional independence occurs relatively early in development, with weaning documented at 42 days since birth [tx = 42 days since birth] under thermoneutral conditions maintained at 34.8 °C [T = 34.8 °C]. This weaning age, inferred from patterns observed in Plecotus auritus, represents the point at which the young begin to consume solid insect prey and terminate their reliance on maternal provisioning. The relatively abbreviated lactation period is consistent with the species' small body size and the high metabolic costs associated with milk production in temperate-zone insectivores.

Reproductive parameters for the eastern long-eared bat are characteristic of a slow-paced life history strategy typical of many small vespertilionids. Based on extrapolations from the well-studied congener Plecotus auritus, females produce a single pup per litter [N_R_i = single pup per litter], and they raise only one litter per year [F_R_i = one litter per year], yielding a maximum reproductive rate of one pup annually [Ri = one pup annually]. This low fecundity is balanced by a gestation period of 65 days [tg = 65 days] when females maintain a body temperature of 34.8 °C [T = 34.8 °C], a duration that is relatively protracted for a bat of this size. The extended gestation likely facilitates the development of relatively well-formed neonates at parturition, a trade-off that reduces postnatal developmental demands on the lactating female. Field records indicate that the timing of parturition is tightly synchronized with seasonal peaks in insect prey abundance.

Sexual maturation in Nyctophilus bifax is delayed relative to the weaning age, reflecting the prolonged period required for juveniles to attain the body size and condition necessary for successful reproduction. Puberty is reached at 365 days since birth [tp = 365 days since birth] under stable thermal conditions of 34.8 °C [T = 34.8 °C], meaning that individuals born in a given summer typically do not become reproductively active until the following breeding season. This extended period of reproductive quiescence is common among temperate-zone vespertilionids and is thought to allow young bats to accumulate sufficient fat reserves for both hibernation and subsequent reproductive effort. The age at first reproduction therefore closely follows the attainment of puberty, with most females breeding for the first time at roughly one year since birth [tR = roughly one year since birth]. This life-history schedule imposes a relatively high premium on adult survival.

Maximum longevity estimates for Nyctophilus bifax indicate a lifespan of 30 years [am = 30 years] under optimal conditions maintained at 34.8 °C [T = 34.8 °C], a figure derived from mark-recapture studies of the closely related Plecotus auritus. Such extended longevity is exceptional for a mammal of this body size and is characteristic of the slow life-history syndrome observed among many bat species. The combination of a single annual offspring, delayed puberty, and a remarkably long lifespan places N. bifax firmly at the slow end of the mammalian life-history continuum. This strategy is thought to be an adaptive response to the high extrinsic mortality risks faced during aerial foraging and the energetic constraints imposed by hibernation over temperate winters. The species' persistence in fragmented landscapes likely depends on the survival of long-lived adults.
